title: A path with many folders that do not exist costs quadratic time at the capability check.
text: [`resolved`] walks up from the path a program named to its deepest existing ancestor, and asks [`Files::canonical`] about every ancestor on the way. Each of those calls reads the whole remaining prefix, so a path whose last `k` components are all missing costs `k` calls over a prefix of `k` components: the work grows with the square of the depth. It is reached whenever an `fs.read` or `fs.write` grant is a list of roots, by every `Core\IO` member that takes a path and by `Core\IO::within`, and the path may be one a request supplied. Doubling the depth multiplies the time by four, a path a few hundred thousand folders deep takes more than a minute on a debug build, and the whole walk is inside one call of the member. The answer itself is right: the path is refused, or allowed and then failed by the operating system, which opens no path that long. Bounding the walk is a new refusal at the capability door, because a path longer than the platform can open would be denied where a root covers it and the operating system's own error is what a program reads today; which bound, per platform, and which error class are a decision and not a slice. Found by `tests/hostile/tools/install/when-something-is-refused/02-a-path-two-million-folders-deep.nvs`, which is still running when its timeout expires and carries this record's marker.
